premise: Most people's intimate lives are limited by one thing: nobody says what they actually want. Not their partner, not them. This campaign is about shame, nerve and plain speech — owning what you want, asking for it, hearing no without collapsing, and being someone another person can be honest with.

reps.label: Said what I wanted
reps.hint: Out loud, to the person it concerns. Any size.

reps.label: Asked what they wanted
reps.hint: And listened to the whole answer.

reps.label: Initiated
reps.hint: Made the first move rather than waiting to be chosen.

reps.label: Sat through the awkward
reps.hint: Stayed in a conversation you wanted to escape.

reps.label: Stated a limit
reps.hint: Said no, or not that, or not yet. Yours or theirs, respected.

principles.title: Silence is the actual problem
principles.body: Very few intimate lives are limited by technique. They are limited by two people each waiting for the other to bring something up. The skill being built here is speech: naming a want, hearing one, and staying in the room while it is uncomfortable.

principles.title: Consent is the whole frame
principles.body: Everything in this campaign assumes an enthusiastic, freely given yes that can be withdrawn at any moment without cost. Asking is not a formality to get past — it is the practice. Anyone who treats a partner's no as an obstacle to route around is not doing this campaign, they are doing something else.

principles.title: Shame keeps the volume low
principles.body: Most people carry a private belief that what they want is strange or too much. Almost always it is ordinary and far more common than they think. Shame is not evidence about the want, it is evidence about how alone you have been with it.

principles.title: Vulnerability, again
principles.body: The same thing that produces attraction produces intimacy: letting someone see the real version while they still have the option to leave. A partner cannot be close to a performance, however well executed.

principles.title: Ask, do not hint
principles.body: Hinting protects you from a clear no while guaranteeing you rarely get a clear yes. It also puts the work of guessing onto someone else. Say the thing. The discomfort lasts seconds; the hinting can last years.

principles.title: A no is not a rejection of you
principles.body: Someone declining something is information about that thing, at that time, for them. Treating it as a verdict on your worth makes you unsafe to be honest with, and a partner who cannot decline safely will stop telling you the truth about anything.

principles.title: Your body is not the obstacle
principles.body: Waiting until you look a certain way before you allow yourself to want things is a way of never starting. Treat your body as something you look after because it is yours, not as an entrance fee. Confidence is a behaviour before it is a feeling.

principles.title: Keep the conversation open
principles.body: One honest conversation is a start, not a fix. What changes an intimate life is making these exchanges ordinary — a thing you do regularly and without ceremony, rather than a crisis meeting held once a year.

missions.do: Write down what you actually want more of. For your eyes only, no editing.
missions.why: You cannot ask for something you have not let yourself name in private first.

missions.do: Read the consent principle before anything else in this campaign.
missions.why: Everything here runs on a freely given yes. Get that clear before you start.

missions.do: Name one thing you have felt ashamed of wanting. Just to yourself.
missions.why: Shame shrinks under description. Say it plainly and watch it get smaller.

missions.do: Do one thing for your body today because it is yours, not because of how it looks.
missions.why: Move it, feed it, rest it. Ownership before appearance.

missions.do: Spend ten minutes undressed, alone, without inspecting yourself for faults.
missions.why: Neutrality is the target, not admiration. Most people never practise it.

missions.do: Notice attraction today without immediately suppressing it.
missions.why: You are allowed to want things. Feeling it is not the same as acting on it.

missions.do: Tell one person something true about yourself that you usually keep back.
missions.why: Practise disclosure somewhere lower stakes than the bedroom first.

missions.do: Say no to something small today without an elaborate excuse.
missions.why: If your no is not real, your yes means nothing. Start with the easy ones.

missions.do: Ask someone a question you would normally consider too personal — respectfully.
missions.why: Calibrate what people are actually willing to talk about. It is more than you think.

missions.do: Book the health thing you have been putting off.
missions.why: Unaddressed physical worry sits underneath a lot of avoidance. Clear it.

missions.do: Tell a partner or someone you are close to one thing you appreciate physically.
missions.why: Specific, spoken, unhedged. Start the habit of saying the unsaid.

missions.do: Ask what they like. Then say nothing until they have finished answering.
missions.why: The listening is the mission. Most people interrupt this conversation to reassure.

missions.do: Name one thing you want, out loud, to the person it concerns.
missions.why: The first plain sentence is the hardest one you will say in this campaign.

missions.do: Initiate something today rather than waiting to be invited.
missions.why: Waiting to be chosen is comfortable and it is why nothing changes.

missions.do: Have the conversation about what is and is not working. Both directions.
missions.why: Ask for their half honestly. This is not a complaint, it is maintenance.

missions.do: Receive a no, or a not tonight, without going quiet or cold.
missions.why: How you take a decline determines whether you are ever told the truth again.

missions.do: State one limit of your own clearly.
missions.why: Boundaries are not rejection. They are the map that makes the yes trustworthy.

missions.do: Say the thing you have been not saying for months.
missions.why: You know which one. It has been getting more expensive the whole time.

missions.do: Ask for something specific rather than something general.
missions.why: "More closeness" cannot be acted on. A specific request can be.

missions.do: Learn something real about bodies or desire from a credible source.
missions.why: Most of what people carry is misinformation absorbed young. Replace some of it.

missions.do: Make one evening deliberately unhurried, with phones out of the room.
missions.why: Attention is the input. Almost nothing here works while you are half elsewhere.

missions.do: Ask afterwards what they liked. Actually ask.
missions.why: Feedback is normal in every other skill. Here people guess for years instead.

missions.do: Try something new that you both agreed to, out loud, beforehand.
missions.why: The agreeing out loud is the mission. Enthusiasm from both sides or it does not happen.

missions.do: Say what you were feeling during, not just afterwards.
missions.why: Real-time honesty is a different muscle from the debrief. Build it.

missions.do: Handle a mismatch in what you each want without making anyone wrong.
missions.why: Two honest people will want different things. That is normal, not a failure.

missions.do: Check in about something you assumed was fine.
missions.why: Assumptions calcify. A single question keeps them from becoming resentments.

missions.do: Tell them what you find attractive about who they are, not how they look.
missions.why: Character is the harder compliment and it lands considerably deeper.

missions.do: Make the honest conversation a standing thing, not an emergency.
missions.why: Schedule it if you have to. Ordinary beats heroic every time.

missions.do: Review it honestly: what changed, what you avoided, what is still unsaid.
missions.why: Count the conversations you had, not the outcomes you engineered.

missions.do: Say the last thing on your list — the one you skipped every time.
missions.why: There is one left. There always is. This campaign was building the nerve for it.
